title: Why 10 beats 9 with three dice (Galileo's answer)
description:
With three dice, 9 and 10 can each be made from six combinations, yet dice players noticed 10 comes up more. Galileo's fix: tell the dice apart. 1-2-6 can land 6 ways, a pair like 1-4-4 only 3, and 3-3-3 just 1, so 9 has 25 of the 216 possible throws and 10 has 27: about 8% more often. Galileo wrote this up in 'On the discoveries of dice', some 400 years ago.

Numbers checked in code (all 216 throws counted, plus a million simulated throws). Source: Galileo, Sopra le scoperte dei dadi (transl. E. H. Thorne), york.ac.uk/depts/maths/histstat/galileo.htm

facts_checked: 9 and 10 each have 6 unordered combinations; 9: 25 of 216 throws, 10: 27 of 216 (11.6% vs 12.5%, 8% more often); 1-2-6 lands 6 ways, 1-4-4 3 ways, 3-3-3 1 way (verify.py; 1,000,000 simulated throws: 0.1155 vs 0.1252)

beats.say: Your dice make 9 and 10 six ways each, yet 10 wins.
The dice aren't loaded, and it isn't luck. Dice players in Galileo's Italy saw it over years of throws. He worked out why.
List the ways to make 9. One, two, six. One, four, four. Three, three, three. And three more. 10 has six too.
Now paint your dice red, blue and green. One, two, six can land six ways: any die shows the one, either of the others the two.
But one, four, four lands only three ways. The one picks a die, and that's it. Three threes land one way.
So six ways was the wrong count. Count the landings.
Out of 216 throws, 10 comes up 27 times, and 9 only 25. 8% more often. Galileo wrote it down about 400 years ago.
So with three dice, which wins: 11 or 12?
